questions.stem: Which of these emits a continuous spectrum by incandescence?
options: The glowing tungsten filament of a light globe
The heated sodium vapour in a street lamp
The low-pressure neon gas in an advertising sign
The excited mercury vapour in a fluorescent tube
questions.explanation: Hot solids, liquids and dense gases emit a continuous range of frequencies, which is incandescence. Low-density heated vapours such as sodium, neon or mercury emit line spectra instead.

questions.stem: As an incandescent object gets hotter, how does its spectrum change?
options: It breaks up into separate bright lines that move to higher frequency
Its peak stays at the same frequency, but the spectrum becomes narrower
It becomes more intense at every frequency, and its peak shifts to higher frequency
It becomes more intense at every frequency, and its peak shifts to lower frequency
questions.explanation: A hotter body radiates more at all frequencies and its peak moves towards higher frequency, so its colour changes from red through orange and yellow towards white. It still gives a continuous spectrum, not lines.

questions.stem: A blacksmith heats two identical iron bars. One glows dull red and the other glows white. What can be concluded?
options: The red-hot bar is at a higher temperature than the white-hot bar
The two bars are at the same temperature but have different surfaces
The white-hot bar is emitting a line spectrum instead of a continuous one
The white-hot bar is at a higher temperature than the red-hot bar
questions.explanation: The dominant colour of an incandescent object depends on its temperature. White light means the spectrum's peak has moved far enough up that all visible colours are strongly emitted, which needs a higher temperature than red.

questions.stem: The voltage across a filament globe is slowly reduced. How does the light change?
options: It changes from a continuous spectrum to a set of separate red lines
It becomes dimmer and redder, as the peak of its spectrum shifts to lower frequency
It becomes dimmer and bluer, as the peak of its spectrum shifts to higher frequency
It becomes dimmer, but its colour stays exactly the same at every voltage
questions.explanation: Less current means a cooler filament. A cooler incandescent source emits less at every frequency and its peak moves to lower frequency, so the light looks dimmer and redder.

questions.stem: When is an atom said to be in an excited state?
options: When its nucleus has absorbed a photon from incident light
When one of its electrons has been raised to a higher energy level
When it has lost one or more of its electrons completely to ionisation
When its electrons are all in their lowest possible energy levels
questions.explanation: An excited atom has an electron in a level above its ground state. Removing an electron completely is ionisation, and all electrons in their lowest levels is the ground state.

questions.stem: A low-pressure gas is bombarded with fast electrons and begins to glow. Why?
options: Collisions split the atoms' nuclei, and the fragments release light as they recombine
Collisions raise electrons in the atoms to higher levels, and photons are emitted as they drop back
Collisions heat the gas until it glows with a continuous spectrum, like a filament globe
The fast electrons themselves turn into photons when they slow down inside the gas
questions.explanation: Atoms can be excited by heating or by bombardment with photons or particles such as electrons. The excited atoms then return to lower levels, emitting photons at the frequencies of their line spectrum.

questions.stem: The light from the heated vapour of a pure element is viewed with a spectrometer. What is seen?
options: A continuous band of colours from red through to violet
A continuous band of colours crossed by a set of dark lines
A single bright line at the frequency of the strongest colour emitted
A set of bright lines at particular frequencies on a dark background
questions.explanation: A heated low-density vapour emits only certain discrete frequencies, giving a line emission spectrum. Dark lines on a continuous band form an absorption spectrum, made when continuous light passes through a cooler gas.

questions.stem: Why can the line emission spectrum of a gas be used to identify the element it contains?
options: Each element emits only one line, at a frequency set by its atomic mass
Each element's lines are brighter than those of every other element
Each element emits a continuous spectrum with its own peak colour
Each element has its own set of energy levels, so its pattern of lines is unique
questions.explanation: The line frequencies are set by the differences between an element's energy levels, which differ from element to element. Matching the lines in a sample to known patterns, like a fingerprint, identifies the elements present.

questions.stem: Element P has lines at 450, 520 and 610 nm; Q at 480 and 560 nm; R at 430, 520 and 670 nm. A gas sample shows lines at 450, 480, 520, 560 and 610 nm only. Which elements are present?
options: Q and R only
P and R only
P and Q only
P, Q and R
questions.explanation: Every line of P (450, 520, 610) and of Q (480, 560) appears. R cannot be present because its 430 nm and 670 nm lines are missing; its 520 nm line is accounted for by P.

questions.stem: What does the presence of discrete frequencies in line emission spectra show about atoms?
options: Atoms emit photons only when their nuclei change energy
Every atom of an element emits all of its lines at once
Electrons in atoms can have only certain discrete energies
Electrons in atoms can have any energy within a continuous range
questions.explanation: Each line is a photon of energy hf equal to the difference between two energy levels. If electron energies could take any value, transitions would produce a continuous spectrum instead of sharp lines.

questions.stem: What is the ground state of an atom?
options: The state in which it has absorbed the most energy it can hold
The state in which its electrons are in their lowest possible energy levels
The state in which an electron has just been removed from the atom
The state in which its electrons have zero energy on the energy-level diagram
questions.explanation: In the ground state the atom has its lowest energy, with all electrons in the lowest levels available. On an energy-level diagram this is the most negative level; zero energy corresponds to ionisation.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.40 eV (n = 2), −1.51 eV (n = 3) and −0.85 eV (n = 4). What is the wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation: ΔE = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so λ = hc/ΔE = 6.58 × 10⁻⁷ m, the red line of hydrogen. Adding the two energies instead of subtracting gives 4.91 eV and 2.53 × 10⁻⁷ m.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.40 eV (n = 2), −1.51 eV (n = 3) and −0.85 eV (n = 4). What is the frequency of the photon emitted when an electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation: ΔE = −0.85 − (−3.40) = 2.55 eV = 4.08 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and f = ΔE/h = 6.15 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Leaving ΔE in electronvolts gives the absurd 3.85 × 10³³ Hz.

questions.stem: Atoms of hydrogen are excited to the n = 4 level. How many different spectral lines can be produced as their electrons return to the ground state by every possible route?
questions.explanation: The possible transitions are 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1, giving six lines. Counting only the drops from n = 4 gives 3.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.40 eV (n = 2), −1.51 eV (n = 3) and −0.85 eV (n = 4). What is the ionisation energy of hydrogen in joules? Use 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation: The ionisation energy is the energy to take an electron from the ground state (−13.6 eV) to 0 eV, which is 13.6 eV = 13.6 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. The value 5.44 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the energy needed from n = 2, not from the ground state.

questions.stem: In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum are the lines of hydrogen produced by transitions that end on the n = 1 level?
options: Visible light
Infrared
Radio
Ultraviolet
questions.explanation: Drops to n = 1 involve the largest energy gaps, at least 10.2 eV, so the photons are ultraviolet. Transitions ending on n = 2 give the visible lines, and those ending on n = 3 are infrared.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.40 eV (n = 2), −1.51 eV (n = 3) and −0.85 eV (n = 4). Why are all the lines produced by transitions ending on n = 3 in the infrared?
options: Every such transition releases more than 10.2 eV, too much for a visible photon
Electrons ending on n = 3 emit two photons that combine into one infrared photon
Transitions ending on n = 3 come from ionised atoms, which emit only infrared
No such transition releases more than 1.51 eV, too little for a visible photon
questions.explanation: The largest possible drop to n = 3 is from 0 eV, releasing 1.51 eV, which corresponds to λ = hc/E ≈ 823 nm, beyond the red end of the visible spectrum. Every other drop to n = 3 releases even less energy.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.40 eV (n = 2), −1.51 eV (n = 3) and −0.85 eV (n = 4). Which transition emits the photon with the longest wavelength?
options: n = 4 to n = 3
n = 3 to n = 2
n = 4 to n = 2
n = 2 to n = 1
questions.explanation: Wavelength is inversely proportional to photon energy, so the longest wavelength comes from the smallest gap. The gap from n = 4 to n = 3 is only 0.66 eV, smaller than 1.89, 2.55 or 10.2 eV.

questions.stem: An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV (ground state), −6.0 eV, −4.0 eV and −1.0 eV. What is its ionisation energy?
options: 1.0 eV
9.0 eV
questions.explanation: Ionisation takes an electron from the ground state, −10.0 eV, to 0 eV, so 10.0 eV is needed. The value 9.0 eV would take it only as far as the −1.0 eV level.

questions.stem: An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV (ground state), −6.0 eV, −4.0 eV and −1.0 eV. Which photon could NOT be absorbed by this atom while it is in its ground state?
options: A 6.0 eV photon
A 9.0 eV photon
A 2.0 eV photon
A 4.0 eV photon
questions.explanation: From the ground state, absorbed photons must match the gaps up to −6.0, −4.0 and −1.0 eV, which are 4.0, 6.0 and 9.0 eV. The 2.0 eV gap is between −6.0 and −4.0 eV, which needs an atom that is already excited.

questions.stem: An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV (ground state), −6.0 eV, −4.0 eV and −1.0 eV. An electron with 7.0 eV of kinetic energy collides with the atom in its ground state. Which kinetic energy could the electron have after the collision?
options: 6.0 eV
1.0 eV
0 eV
4.0 eV
questions.explanation: Unlike a photon, a colliding electron can give up part of its energy. It can excite the atom by 4.0 eV or 6.0 eV, leaving 3.0 eV or 1.0 eV, or bounce off with all 7.0 eV. It cannot give 7.0 eV, because no gap from the ground state equals 7.0 eV.

questions.stem: White light passes through a cool gas of a single element and is then viewed with a spectrometer. What is seen?
options: Bright lines at particular frequencies on a completely dark background
A continuous spectrum that is evenly dimmer at every frequency
A continuous spectrum with extra bright lines added to it
A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines at particular frequencies
questions.explanation: Atoms of the gas absorb only the photons whose energies match their energy gaps, removing those frequencies and leaving dark lines. This is a line absorption spectrum.

questions.stem: Why do the dark lines in a gas's absorption spectrum appear at only some of the frequencies of its emission lines?
options: Most atoms in a cool gas are in the ground state, so only transitions up from it occur
Absorbed photons are always re-emitted at the same frequency in the same direction
Absorption needs photons of higher frequency than those emitted by the gas
Only the brightest emission lines are strong enough to be absorbed
questions.explanation: Emission lines come from drops between many pairs of levels in a hot gas. In a cool gas nearly all atoms are in the ground state, so only photons matching jumps up from that level are absorbed, a subset of the emission lines.

questions.stem: Why does hydrogen at room temperature show no absorption lines in the visible region?
options: Its atoms are ionised at room temperature, so they cannot absorb any photons
Visible photons pass between hydrogen atoms without ever meeting one
Its atoms are in n = 1, and every jump up from n = 1 needs an ultraviolet photon
Its atoms are in n = 2, and every jump up from n = 2 needs an infrared photon
questions.explanation: The visible hydrogen lines involve the n = 2 level. At room temperature almost all atoms are in n = 1, and the smallest jump up from there, to n = 2, needs 10.2 eV, an ultraviolet photon.

questions.stem: What produces the dark Fraunhofer lines in the spectrum of sunlight?
options: Sunspots block particular frequencies of light from leaving the Sun's surface
The Sun's magnetic field bends particular frequencies of light away from the Earth
Cooler gases in the Sun's outer layers absorb particular frequencies of the continuous light below
Hot gases in the Sun's core emit particular frequencies more strongly than the rest
questions.explanation: The dense, hot interior of the Sun emits a continuous spectrum. Atoms in the cooler outer layers absorb the frequencies matching their energy gaps, leaving dark lines that reveal which elements are present.

questions.stem: Atoms that absorb light to form an absorption line soon re-emit photons of the same energy. Why does the line still look dark?
options: The re-emitted photons always have a lower frequency, so they appear elsewhere
The re-emitted photons are absorbed again by the spectrometer's glass
The re-emitted photons cancel the incoming photons by destructive interference
The re-emitted photons go off in all directions, so few continue along the original beam
questions.explanation: Absorbed energy is re-emitted in random directions, so very little of it continues towards the observer. The line is not completely black, but it is much fainter than the continuous spectrum around it.

questions.stem: In one type of fluorescence, what happens to an atom?
options: An atom absorbs one photon, then emits one identical photon in the same direction
An atom absorbs heat, then emits a continuous spectrum of visible light
An atom absorbs one photon, then emits two or more photons of lower energy
An atom absorbs two photons, then emits one photon of higher energy
questions.explanation: The electron is raised by one photon, then returns in two or more smaller steps, each emitting a lower-energy, longer-wavelength photon. Emitting an identical photon in the same direction is stimulated emission.

questions.stem: A banknote has a pattern that glows green under an ultraviolet lamp. Which explanation fits?
options: Atoms combine the energy of several ultraviolet photons into one green photon
Atoms absorb ultraviolet photons and return to lower levels in steps, emitting visible photons
Atoms absorb green light from the room and re-emit it when the lamp is turned on
The ultraviolet light heats the ink until it glows green by incandescence
questions.explanation: In fluorescence one high-energy ultraviolet photon raises an electron, which returns by smaller steps that release lower-energy photons, some of them visible. A green photon has less energy than the ultraviolet photon absorbed.

questions.stem: An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV (ground state), −6.0 eV, −4.0 eV and −1.0 eV. A ground-state atom absorbs a 6.0 eV photon, then returns to the ground state by fluorescence. Which pair of photons does it emit?
options: 2.0 eV and 4.0 eV
3.0 eV and 3.0 eV
6.0 eV and 6.0 eV
1.0 eV and 5.0 eV
questions.explanation: The photon raises the electron from −10.0 to −4.0 eV. Returning through the −6.0 eV level releases 2.0 eV and then 4.0 eV. Two 3.0 eV photons are impossible because there is no level at −7.0 eV.

questions.stem: What is spontaneous emission?
options: An incoming photon makes an excited electron drop, giving two identical photons
An electron absorbs a photon and rises to a higher energy level
An electron leaves a metal surface when a photon strikes it
An excited electron drops to a lower level of its own accord, emitting a photon
questions.explanation: Excited states are generally short-lived, and electrons return to lower levels without any trigger, emitting photons in random directions and phases. When an incoming photon triggers the drop, the process is stimulated emission.

questions.stem: How does a photon from stimulated emission compare with the photon that stimulated it?
options: Lower in energy, but travelling in the same direction
Identical in direction, but with twice the energy
Identical in energy, direction and phase
Identical in energy, but travelling in a random direction
questions.explanation: The incident photon, whose energy matches the transition, triggers the drop and the new photon is an exact copy of it. Photons from spontaneous emission, by contrast, go in random directions with random phases.

questions.stem: What is a population inversion in a set of atoms?
options: The atoms have swapped the order of their upper and lower energy levels
More atoms are in a higher-energy state than in a lower-energy state
More atoms are in the ground state than in any excited state
All the atoms have been ionised by a strong electric field
questions.explanation: Normally most atoms are in lower states. A population inversion reverses this for a particular pair of levels, which is needed for a laser to work.

questions.stem: Light of exactly the right frequency passes through a set of atoms. What must be true for stimulated emission to predominate over absorption?
options: The atoms must be cooled so that none of them are excited
More atoms must be in the upper level of the transition than in the lower level
More atoms must be in the lower level of the transition than in the upper level
The light must be more intense than sunlight at the Earth's surface
questions.explanation: A matching photon is absorbed by an atom in the lower level but causes stimulated emission from one in the upper level. Only when the upper level holds more atoms, a population inversion, are photons added faster than they are removed.

questions.stem: Why must the upper level used in a practical laser be metastable?
options: Its short lifetime makes atoms drop back very quickly, so many more photons are produced
It is the only level that can absorb photons from the pumping light
It is the level from which the atom is ionised to release electrons
Its long lifetime lets atoms build up there, so a population inversion can form
questions.explanation: Most excited states last only a very short time, so atoms leave them before enough accumulate. A metastable state lasts much longer, allowing more atoms to collect there than in the lower level.

questions.stem: How does stimulated emission produce coherent light in a laser?
options: Each stimulated photon is in phase with its trigger, so the copies build up in step
Each atom emits photons at random, but the mirrors then sort them all into the same phase
The pumping energy forces every atom to emit at exactly the same instant
The laser tube filters out every photon that is not of the right colour
questions.explanation: Each new photon matches its trigger in energy, direction and phase, and goes on to stimulate further identical photons. The result is a growing beam of photons all in step, which is coherent light.

questions.stem: Which set of properties describes laser light?
options: Coherent and made of a continuous range of wavelengths
Incoherent and spread evenly in all directions from the source
Coherent and monochromatic, and it may be of high intensity
Incoherent and monochromatic, and always of low intensity
questions.explanation: Laser light is coherent (in phase), monochromatic (a single wavelength) and can be very intense. A light globe, by contrast, gives incoherent light over a range of wavelengths in all directions.

questions.stem: Why can a 5 mW laser pointer damage the eye when a 5 W torch usually does not?
options: The laser's light is incoherent, so it heats the retina more evenly
The laser's energy is concentrated in a narrow beam that the eye focuses to a tiny spot
The laser's photons each carry more energy than all the photons from the torch
The laser emits ultraviolet light, which the torch's glass lens filters out
questions.explanation: A laser beam barely spreads, so its power stays concentrated in a small area, and the eye's lens focuses it to a tiny spot on the retina. The torch spreads its power over a wide area, so far less reaches any one point.

questions.stem: Which practice is part of the safe handling of lasers?
options: Checking that the beam is working by looking briefly into it from a distance
Aiming the beam at shiny surfaces so that it is easier for others to see
Keeping the beam at eye height so that its path is easy to follow
Wearing eye protection rated for the laser's wavelength and never looking along the beam
questions.explanation: Lasers must never be viewed directly, protective eyewear must suit the wavelength, and reflective surfaces must be avoided or controlled. Beams should be kept below eye level, not at it.
